prime.problem: Every sort has to decide how much work nearly sorted input deserves. A sort that ignores existing order does n² or n log n work on data that is only a few swaps from done, and on tiny arrays the clever sorts' bookkeeping costs more than the sorting.
prime.fits: First sort of the course. It builds on cs-1's big-O, and its swap count (inversions) comes back in counting during a merge and in the n log n card's compare table.
expect: why Timsort uses it for short runs
prime.goal: Predict insertion sort's swaps and compares on any small array from its inversions, and say when it beats an n log n sort.

attend: Why does swapping two adjacent out-of-order neighbours remove exactly one inversion, and never create another?
On a, keys 27 and 3 reach index 0. Why does that make the compare count 15 instead of 17?
Which single character in the loop decides whether the sort is stable?
Why does Timsort still use this O(n²) sort inside an O(n log n) algorithm?
The 3,185× gap to sorted() mixes two causes. Which two?

must: Adjacent swap of an out-of-order pair → fixes exactly that pair, leaves all others' order unchanged → swaps = inversions → 0 on sorted input, n(n − 1)/2 on reversed, n(n − 1)/4 on average

Each key stops at the first neighbour that isn't bigger → one extra compare per key except those that slide to index 0 → compares = inv + (n − 1) − f (11 + 6 − 2 = 15 on a) → nearly sorted input costs about n

Work tracks disorder, not size → tiny or nearly sorted runs cost almost nothing, while n log n sorts pay recursion and buffer overhead → Timsort extends short runs to minrun (32–64) with binary insertion sort
elevated: Strict a[j - 1] > a[j] → a key never jumps over an equal one → stable; >= breaks stability and adds swaps on duplicates
reference: measured 0.828 s vs 0.00026 s at n = 5,000
selection and bubble sort compare counts on a

compress.prompt: In 3–4 sentences from memory: what insertion sort's loop does, why its cost equals the number of inversions, and why that makes it the right sort for tiny or nearly sorted input but the wrong one for 5,000 random items.
checklist: sorted prefix; each new key swaps left past bigger neighbours
each adjacent swap removes exactly one inversion, so swaps = inversions
sorted input: 0 swaps, n − 1 compares; reversed: n(n − 1)/2
stable because of the strict comparison
Timsort uses it for runs under 32–64; random large input is O(n²)

retrieve.q: Explain why insertion sort is called adaptive, in terms of what its work actually counts.
answer: the work is one swap per inversion plus about one stopping compare per key
inversions measure disorder: 0 when sorted, n(n − 1)/2 when reversed
so cost is O(n + inversions), close to n on nearly sorted data

retrieve.q: Trace the step where key 10 (i = 6) is inserted into [3, 9, 27, 38, 43, 82]: which values does it jump over, how many swaps and compares, and why does it stop where it does?
answer: 5 compares: four that trigger swaps plus 9 > 10? no, which stops it

retrieve.q: You must keep a leaderboard of 64 scores sorted as scores trickle in one by one. Insertion sort, or re-running an n log n sort each time? What does each cost per new score, and what would change your answer?
answer: insertion: one new key is at most n inversions, so ≤ 64 swaps, and it's online
re-sorting pays n log n every time and ignores that the list was already sorted
at huge n with random arrivals, a heap or balanced tree avoids the O(n) shift

compare.q: Both cards count inversions of a and get 11. What is fundamentally different about how they find them, and when does the difference matter?
answer: insertion sort removes inversions one adjacent swap at a time: O(n + inv), up to O(n²)
the merge counts a whole block of right-half elements at once when a left element is placed: O(n log n) always
for n = 10⁵ random input: ≈ 2.5 × 10⁹ swaps vs ≈ 1.7 × 10⁶ element moves

compare.q: Insertion sort does 6 compares on sorted a, below the 13-compare floor for n = 7. Why doesn't that contradict the lower bound?
answer: the bound is about the worst input over all 5,040 orders; insertion's worst is 21
a sort may be fast on some inputs as long as some input forces ≥ log₂ n! compares
adaptivity exploits inputs whose order is already mostly known

predict.q: Change the inner test to a[j - 1] >= a[j] and sort [2, 1, 2, 2]. Predict the swap count for each version and whether the relative order of the three 2s survives.
predict.answer: Strict >: only the pair (2, 1) is an inversion, so 1 swap, and the 2s keep their order (stable). With >=, each later 2 also swaps past every equal 2 before it: 1 swap for the 1, then the third 2 jumps one 2 and the fourth jumps two, 4 swaps in total, and the 2s end up reversed. Equal keys are treated as inversions, so the sort is no longer stable and does extra work.
